messages.body_plain:
Hello Group,

What if you want model-averaged predictions but have multiple categorical covariates? I have attached a simple .csv data file to go along with the code below where I would like to get abundance estimates for a range of values for 'size' while averaging the 'wetland' and 'disturbance' variables. Any help would be greatly appreciated. This example uses the gmultmix function, but could apply to any unmarked function.

Cheers,
Dan

library(unmarked)

# BRING IN DATA, SET UP PIFUN, OBSTOY & UMF
data<-read.csv("TEST.csv")

# piFun
depDoublePiFun <- function(p) {
    M <- nrow(p)
    pi <- matrix(NA, M, 2)
    pi[,1] <- p[,1]
    pi[,2] <- p[,2]*(1-p[,1])
    return(pi)
}

#obsToY
obsToY <- matrix(1, 2, 2)
numPrimary <- 1
obsToY <- kronecker(diag(numPrimary), obsToY)

y<-as.matrix(subset(data,select=c(y.1,y.2)))
site.covs<-data.frame(size=data$size,wetland=data$wetland,disturbance=data$disturbance)
umf<-unmarkedFrameGMM(y=y, siteCovs=site.covs,numPrimary=numPrimary, obsToY=obsToY, piFun="depDoublePiFun")
summary(umf)

# RUN SOME MODELS

m1<-gmultmix(~size, ~1, ~1, umf)
m2<-gmultmix(~size+wetland, ~1, ~1, umf)
m3<-gmultmix(~size+disturbance, ~1, ~1, umf)
m4<-gmultmix(~size+wetland+disturbance, ~1, ~1, umf)

fms <- fitList( "m1"=m1,"m2"=m2,"m3"=m3,"m4"=m4); modSel(fms)# Model Selection

# MODEL AVERAGING USING PREDICT

# estimates using 'm1'
newData1<-data.frame(size=seq(0,1,length=9))
predict(m1, type="lambda", newdata=newData1,appendData=TRUE)

# estimates using 'm2' # could be used in model-averaging when only one categorical variable exists #
newData2<-data.frame(size=seq(0,1,length=9), disturbance=(c("X","Y","Z")))
contrasts(newData2$disturbance) <- matrix(1/3, 3, 2) # define custom contrasts
predict(m3, type="lambda", newdata=newData2,appendData=TRUE)

# How do you use predict to get model-averaged results (using 'fms') when you
# have two categorigal variables / factors?

Hi Richard,

Thanks much for your reply. I checked out your suggestion which was in line with the example presented in the colext() vignette (Kery and Chandler 2012) but I simply couldn't make it work. Following this code:

  unused argument(s) (date = seq(4, 282, length = 282))

I tried other permutations of  this variety and can't figure it out.  My intent was to plot detection probability as a function of Julian date while holding all other factors in the model constant (zero). To move forward, I came up with this alternative solution that removed all the other covariates in the detection process, leaving "date" (data.frame of 9 columns) as the sole covariate that influenced detection.

detect <- colext(~1,~1,~1,~date,data=umf)
nd  <- data.frame(date=seq(4,282,length=282))
E.p <- predict(detect, type="det", newdata=nd, appendData=TRUE)

##Plot it:
with(E.p,{
  plot(date,Predicted,ylim=c(0,0.65),type="l",
       xlab="Julian Date",
       ylab=expression(italic(p)),cex.lab=0.8,cex.axis=0.8)
  lines(date,Predicted+1.96*SE,col="black", lty=2,lwd=1)
  lines(date,Predicted-1.96*SE,col="black", lty=2,lwd=1)
  legend("topleft",c("Fitted Regression Line", "95% Confidence Interval"),
         bty="n",lty=c(1,2),lwd=c(1,1),col=c("black","black"),cex=0.8)
})

The plot (attached) makes sense to me. Not the prettiest code or the most sophisticated solution but I believe it gets it done.

My question: by removing the other detection covariates in the best fit model (levels I intended to set to 0) and focusing solely on detection probability by date am I losing detection information that would be used with this abbreviated model and the possible solution you provided below?

I think the answer is "clunky but OK" but wanted to check back with you.

Thanks so much, Erik

detect <- colext(~1,~1,~1,~date,data=umf)
nd  <- data.frame(date=seq(4,282,length=282))
E.p <- predict(detect, type="det", newdata=nd, appendData=TRUE)

with(E.p,{
  plot(date,Predicted,ylim=c(0,0.65),type="l",
       xlab="Julian Date",

  lines(date,Predicted+1.96*SE,col="black", lty=2,lwd=1)

})

Say for example I have 8 models (listed below) that each have different combinations of covariates (2 continuous, 2 categorical) influencing psi. #Sites: 31

#elev.site=700:1600
#rip.site=0:1.5
#res.site='low', 'none'
#burn.site='C', 'E', 'I'

m1 <- colext(~burn.site, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)
m2 <- colext(~res.site, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)
m3 <- colext(~burn.site + res.site, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)
m4 <- colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)

m7 <- colext(~burn.site + scale(rip.site), ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)
m8 <- colext(~res.site + scale(rip.site), ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)

fmList <- fitList(m1=m1, m2=m2, m3=m3, m4=m4, m5=m5, m6=m6, m7=m7, m8=m8)
modSel(fmList)

mod.pred

                           res.site=factor('low', levels=c("low", "none")))
mod.pred <- predict(fmList, type='psi', newdata=data.predict, appendData=TRUE)
mod.pred

#But, I get this error:
Error in X[i, ] : subscript out of bounds

Any insights on how to get these estimates so I can present them in a figure, or should I compare a simpler set of models?  I would really appreciate your help.

Thanks.

messages.body_plain: A Poisson regression models the expected count in a given sample, so if you want densities you just have to do the conversion based on the area of your sample (e.g., plot size).  If the plot size changes across sampling units you need to include the log of plot size as a covariate for abundance (or as an offset, if that's available in multinomPois).  Then your expected count is the number of individuals in a plot with a unit area of 1.

messages.body_plain:
The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach (Switzerland) is seeking a
highly motivated post-doctoral researcher to model large-scale population
processes in Swiss breeding birds. The project is funded by the Swiss
National Science Foundation and aims 1) to develop methods that allow
the estimation of survival and recruitment from monitoring data and 2)
to model spatial and temporal variation of survival and recruitment in
selected species to better understand population trends.

The main data source in the project will be the Swiss breeding bird survey
(MHB), which has been producing 2-3 replicated counts per breeding season
in 267 1 km2 quadrats in every breeding season since 1999. These data
allow estimation of population trends in abundance while accommodating
imperfect detection. However, the demographic mechanisms underlying
these trends remain unknown. The model of Dail and Madsen (Biometrics
2011) enables the estimation of survival and recruitment from such
data. Exploring the potential of the Dail-Madsen-model at the scale
of Switzerland will be a first part of the project. A possible topic
is also to develop extensions of the model, such as the inclusion of
correlated spatial effects or the integration of MHB data with other
data sets that are directly informative about demographic rates, such
as ring-recoveries. A second part of the project is the application of
the modelling framework to address relevant ecological and management
questions. Candidates include the patterns of survival and recruitment
along the altitudinal gradient in Switzerland or whether particular
habitat types or regions are associated with higher survival or
recruitment. It will be one of the duties of the selected candidate
to identify relevant research topics in this field and then to expand
on the identified issues using our data and the modelling framework to
be developed.

The ideal candidate has solid experience in population modelling, in
Bayesian statistical modelling and is a proficient programmer in the R and
BUGS languages. Further, a demonstrated ability and willingness to produce
high-quality publications will be an important selection criterion.

The work will be conducted in collaboration with Michael Schaub
(michael...@vogelwarte.ch) and Marc Kéry (marc...@vogelwarte.ch),
which both are available for further information.

The position is initially for two years, but may be extended to a third
year. The ideal starting date would be June 2013. Information on the
Institute can be found at www.vogelwarte.ch/startseite-english.html <http://www.vogelwarte.ch/startseite-english.html>

Applications (preferably by e-mail) should be submitted to Michael
Schaub (michael...@vogelwarte.ch)
, Swiss Ornithological Institute,
6204 Sempach, Switzerland, before 30 April 2013 and include a letter
of motivation detailing research interests and experiences, a current
CV and contact information of three academic referees. Interviews will
tentatively take place in May 2013.

I was wondering about the temporal scale of your sampling protocol and also about how you integrated the removal counts from the two surveys per year in the first analysis. We wrote a paper  (Kery and Royle, Journal of Animal Ecology, 2010, Hierarchical modelling and estimation of abundance and population trends in metapopulation designs) where we compared multinomial and binomial mixture models for the same original data (detection histories of individual territories). Also, the paper by Nichols, Conn and Thomas (EES, 2009) may be relevant, as it gives a clear overview about which components of detection (e.g., availability, strict detection) are included in the "p" of several methods for estimation of population size.

messages.subject_clean: hierarchical distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked ones and hello Kevin,

here is a question that Kevin Brinck asked outside of the forum, but which I find interesting and relevant for people in this forum, so I copy it here and try to give an answer.

--------- Start original question -----------------
I have a question about state space models as described in chapter 5 of your 2012 book.

We have a 26-year time series of bird abundances where year-to-year estimates vary in biologically implausible ways. Partitioning the variation as you do in your book results in state-process population trajectories that are much more reasonable.

However, our bird abundances are not simple counts. To attempt to account for varying observers and survey conditions we use program Distance to produce annual abundance estimates -- and Distance reports standard errors for those abundances. I have attempted to incorporate that additional information by using the reported precision for each year's observation error, rather than a global estimate (in your code, tau.obs is replaced with tau.obs[t], an additional vector supplied as input).

The Distance-estimated standard errors are large -- so large that there is little variation left for the process term so the state-process trajectory is essentially a straight line, which is also biologically implausible. My question is twofold:

1) Is this an appropriate way of incorporating our extra information on annual uncertainty?
2) How should we interpret the result of little or no process variation?
--------- End original question -----------------

I find this an interesting problem. First of all, yes, your approach seems reasonable to me: you provide the squared standared error estimates from Distance as data and no longer estimate any observation error in the time-series state-space model.

Second, the partitioning of the process and observation variance in these kinds of time-series state-space models is far from straightforward; see for instance the paper by Knape (2008) and also some comments in chapter 5 of the BPA book. Perhaps a very large observation error can simply swamp your process error estimate (but then, you only estimate one of them in your analysis, so perhaps that is not a reasonable suggestion ?).

Finally, and this is my reason for porting your question to this list, in lieu of an integrated analysis, you do a two-step analysis: first estimate the N's and then putting them into a second analysis for modeling structure among them. Bill Link (JWM, 1999, "Modeling structure among params..") calls this statistics on statistics. Often, there is nothing wrong with this approach and often may be the only practically doable one. However, an integrated analysis is probably better, because it probably uses all the information at once (rather than dividing it up into all the annual analyses) and may also get the covariances among params "more" right.

What you really want to do is a hierarchical distance sampling analysis. You want a hierarchical model with a distance sampling observation error at the base plus a model for the variation among the latent abundance states over the 26 years. I haven't seen this kind of model published but a close relative are the HDS models by Hedley and Buckland (2004), Royle et al. (Ecology, 2004), Sillett et al. (EcolAppl, 2012) and a couple of related ones (e.g., Johnson et al. Biometrics, Conn et al. Plos one, I believe). All of these papers deal with distance sampling data at a collection of sites, in a protocol comparable to the classical site-occupancy models for instance. These models can be fit in unmarked using the gdistsamp() function. I don't know program Distance enough, but these models may now be fit there as well. Plus, there are a couple of R packages specifically for hierarchical distance sampling, one by Johnson et al. and another by Conn et al.

I think that you could treat time (your 26 years) as a surrogate for space. Using time as a surrogate for space in these kinds of hierarchical models has been done a couple of times (for instance by Yamaura et al., JAPPL, 2011) and seems to be kosher. So I would suggest to you to fit an integrated analysis using hierarchical distance sampling. To test for a trend (or other simple changes over time), you could fit linear models into the component model for abundance.

It may of course still be that you don't find much variation among the years, but at least you have tried in what must be a more efficient analysis than your current two-step analysis. Also, I am only half a fan of these time-series state-space models for data such as yours, in part because such "implicit hierarchical models" have such a vague description of the observation process ("counts are sometimes too high and sometimes too low relative to the expected count N*p"). In contrast, "explicit hierarchical models"  such as the N-mixture model or hierarchical distance sampling models have a much cleaner and more mechanistic description of the observation process and consequently also latent states with a clear biological meaning (abundance N, instead of expected abundance N*p).

Kind regards  --  Marc

messages.subject_clean: Detection probability varies between models with the same detection covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

I have no experience with distance sampling estimates, but I think the reason is that detection and abundance are estimated simultaneously with a joint likelihood function. Therefore, different covariates in any part of the model can affect the estimates of the other part of the model. Basically, the variation in counts is getting divided up between the two parts of the model (and the error terms) so when the abundance/density covariates are reduced it's possible that some of that uncertainty gets pulled out in detection.

I hope that makes sense and that I'm not too far off the mark. Someone who has more knowledge of the subject can chime in to correct me.
Cheers,
Dan

  The detection rates still differ for a null and global abundance model when I use fewer detection covariates, but the difference is smaller (e.g., 0.31 versus 0.26 with a single detection covariate). Hi Andrew,

Since you get the same AIC and estimates, it sounds like you have
found the global optimum. I was wondering if you get similar results
with a different detection function, such as the half-normal. But
after looking at your original code more carefully, I think the
problem has to due with how you are computing detection probability.
When you have covariates on "sigma" (this should actually be called
the scale parameter), then you can't do:

shape<-exp(coef(Model1,type="det"))

Instead, you need to use predict to give you a value of sigma for
specified covariate values. Then you can plug this value of sigma into
the equation for p.

Richard
